introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0755 Geology 1, JUNE 2026, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, 1 hour 30 minutes. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0755 GEOLOGY - 1'; fill in the information required in the spaces above and on the answer sheet (Candidate Number and Name, Centre Number and Name). Answer ALL the 50 questions. All questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is correct, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet, using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following explains the origin of the Solar System?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Nebular theory** (Kant, 1755, and Laplace, 1796) explains the origin of the Solar System: the Sun and the planets formed together from a single rotating cloud (nebula) of gas and dust that contracted under gravity, flattened into a spinning disc, condensed in the centre to form the Sun, while the planets grew from the material of the disc. The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the whole Universe, not of one planetary system. 'Universal theory' is not an accepted theory of the origin of the Solar System. The Planetesimal hypothesis (Chamberlin and Moulton) is a rival historical hypothesis, which needs a close passage of another star and is no longer accepted in that form; the modern accepted model is the nebular one.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
What is the main cause of the Big Bang?

*Options as printed:* A) High pressure within the system   B) High temperature within the system   C) Presence of electrons within the system   D) The clustering of stars within the system
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Big Bang model describes the expansion of the Universe from an initial state that was extremely **hot and dense**: all the matter and energy were concentrated in a tiny volume at a very high temperature, and the sudden expansion is attributed to this extreme thermal energy of the primordial state (the very high pressure is the consequence of the very high temperature and density). Strictly speaking, science does not know what 'caused' the Big Bang. The presence of electrons (C) is a consequence, and the clustering of stars (D) came hundreds of millions of years after the Big Bang, so neither can be a cause. Options A and B both describe the initial state, which makes the question ambiguous; the high temperature is retained as the intended answer.

**Intended answer: B (High temperature within the system).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the sketch below (Figure 1), which shows the upper 670 km of the Earth, and answer questions 3 and 4.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: upper 670 km of the Earth (continental crust A above the 35 km line, layer B between 35 km and 70 km, depth marks 35 km, 70 km, 200 km (dashed), 400 km and 670 km; brace y from the surface to 70 km, brace x from 70 km to about 200 km; Sea Level shown at the top). Used for questions 3 and 4.*

Identify the discontinuity that exists at a depth of 35 km.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 1 the line at 35 km separates the crust (A) from the mantle (B). This crust-mantle boundary, found at about 35 km under the continents (and only 5 to 10 km under the oceans), is the **Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho)**, recognised by a sudden increase of the P-wave velocity. The Conrad discontinuity lies inside the continental crust (between the upper and lower crust), the Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer core from the inner core at about 5 150 km and the Gutenberg discontinuity is the mantle-outer core boundary at about 2 900 km.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 1 (the same figure as for question 3).

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: upper 670 km of the Earth (continental crust A above the 35 km line, layer B between 35 km and 70 km, depth marks 35 km, 70 km, 200 km (dashed), 400 km and 670 km; brace y from the surface to 70 km, brace x from 70 km to about 200 km; Sea Level shown at the top). Used for questions 3 and 4.*

What is the physical state of the layer labelled Y?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 1 the brace printed 'y' at the top of the section covers the interval from the surface down to 70 km, that is the crust (A) and the uppermost mantle (B): this is the **lithosphere**, the cold, strong outer shell of the Earth. It is **solid and rigid** (it breaks by faulting and carries the plates). The asthenosphere, below it (brace x, 70 km to about 200 km), is the weak layer that behaves plastically, and only the outer core is molten. 'Elastic' describes how the lithosphere transmits seismic waves, not its physical state.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 below illustrates schematically Time - Distance plots for three different types of earthquake waves, labelled X, Y and Z. Use the curves to answer questions 5 and 6.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: time-distance plots (time in s on the vertical axis, 0 to about 30 s; distance in km on the horizontal axis, 0 to 40 km) for three types of earthquake waves X (thick straight line, steepest), Y (curve) and Z (lowest curve). Used for questions 5 and 6.*

Determine the velocity of the wave labelled Y at point 25 km from point 0.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The velocity of a wave is distance divided by travel time, $v = \dfrac{d}{t}$. On the curve Y, the distance of 25 km corresponds to a travel time of about 15 to 16 s (the curve passes through about 14 s near 22 km and reaches 20 s near 40 km). Hence

$$
v = \frac{25\ \mathrm{km}}{15.5\ \mathrm{s}} \approx 1.6\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}
$$

The other options (375, 55 and 750 km/s) are physically impossible for earthquake waves near the surface (typical speeds are 1 to 8 km/s).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 2 (the same figure as for question 5).

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: time-distance plots (time in s on the vertical axis, 0 to about 30 s; distance in km on the horizontal axis, 0 to 40 km) for three types of earthquake waves X (thick straight line, steepest), Y (curve) and Z (lowest curve). Used for questions 5 and 6.*

The curve represented by the letter Z corresponds to:
questions.corrige_markdown:
On a time-distance graph, the wave that needs the least time to reach a given distance is the fastest. Curve Z lies lowest (about 9 s at 25 km), so Z is the first arrival: the **P-waves** (primary, compressional waves), which are the fastest body waves. Curve Y (about 16 s at 25 km) is slower, so it is the S-waves (secondary, shear waves, slower than the P-waves), and the thick straight line X (about 25 s at 25 km), the last to arrive, is a surface wave (L-waves, or Rayleigh waves), the slowest of all.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A crystal face in the Tetragonal system has as Miller Index (111). To what form does this face belong?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the tetragonal system the crystallographic axes are $a_1 = a_2 \neq c$, all at right angles. A face with Miller index (111) cuts the three axes (intercepts 1, 1, 1) at the unit distance, so it is an inclined face that closes the crystal at the top: it belongs to a **bipyramid**, and since it cuts both lateral axes $a_1$ and $a_2$ it is the **bipyramid of the first order** $\{111\}$. The bipyramid of the second order is $\{101\}$ (face parallel to one lateral axis). A pinacoid has the index (001) (or (100)) and is parallel to two axes. The tetrahedron is a form of the cubic system.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Carefully study the crystal drawing below (Figure 3) and answer questions 8 and 9.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: crystal drawing with three faces labelled X (top), Y (front) and Z (left side). Used for questions 8 and 9.*

What is the diagnostic characteristic of this crystal?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Figure 3 is a **rhombohedron**: six faces which are all rhombuses (X, Y and Z are three of them), the faces being equivalent in pairs, and a long diagonal joining two opposite apices. The rhombohedron belongs to the trigonal system, whose diagnostic element of symmetry is **one vertical three-fold axis** (the axis along the long diagonal, parallel to $c$). Four 3-fold axes (A) are the diagnostic of the cubic system, three 2-fold axes at right angles (C) that of the orthorhombic system and one vertical four-fold axis (D) that of the tetragonal system.

**Answer: B.**

One vertical three - fold axis of symmetry
Three two - fold axes of symmetry
One four - fold vertical axis of symmetry

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 3 (the same figure as for question 8).

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: crystal drawing with three faces labelled X (top), Y (front) and Z (left side). Used for questions 8 and 9.*

Which form is represented by the crystal above?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The six faces of the crystal are rhombuses (parallelograms with four equal sides, with no right angle), obtained by drawing the cube stretched or squeezed along a body diagonal. This form is the **rhombohedron** (calcite cleavage fragments are the standard example). A cube has six square faces, a rhombic dodecahedron has twelve rhombic faces and a scalenohedron has twelve scalene triangular faces.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following properties is diagnostic of the Mica group of minerals?
questions.corrige_markdown:
All the micas (muscovite, biotite, phlogopite) have a **perfect basal cleavage** {001}, so that they split into thin, flexible, elastic sheets: this is the property by which a mica is recognised in a hand specimen. A colourless streak (B), a vitreous or pearly lustre (C) and a low specific gravity of about 2.7 to 3.1 (D) are shared with many other minerals (quartz, calcite, feldspars...) and are not diagnostic. Biotite, moreover, is dark and has a pale grey streak.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 4) shows a section of a silicate mineral cut at right angles to the length of the crystal. Use this diagram to answer questions 11 and 12.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: cross-section of a silicate mineral cut at right angles to the length of the crystal: six-sided outline with faces labelled 010, 110, (1-10) and (-1-10) and two sets of cleavage traces. Used for questions 11 and 12.*

The cleavage planes drawn above are typical of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The section is six-sided (bounded by the prism faces 110 and 010) and carries two sets of cleavage traces which cross at about $56^\circ$ and $124^\circ$ (about $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ on the drawing): this is the cleavage of the amphiboles, here **hornblende**. A pyroxene has a nearly square or eight-sided section with two cleavages at about $87^\circ$ and $93^\circ$ (nearly at right angles). Biotite has a single perfect basal cleavage and olivine has no good cleavage.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 4 (the same figure as for question 11).

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: cross-section of a silicate mineral cut at right angles to the length of the crystal: six-sided outline with faces labelled 010, 110, (1-10) and (-1-10) and two sets of cleavage traces. Used for questions 11 and 12.*

The mineral in question 11 has a:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hornblende is an amphibole, an inosilicate in which the silica tetrahedra are linked into **double chains** (repeating unit $\mathrm{Si_4O_{11}}$, the two chains being linked by shared oxygens), which explains the two cleavages at about $56^\circ$ and $124^\circ$ between the chains. The micas have a sheet structure, the feldspars and quartz a framework structure and the pyroxenes a single chain structure.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 5) shows a sequence of rocks in an area formed during volcanic activity. The upper part of each basalt contains vesicles. Study it and answer questions 13 and 14.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: sequence of volcanic rocks, from the base: Tuffs, Ignimbrite (an erosional surface is marked at the top of the Tuffs), a thin unlabelled hatched band, Basalt 1, Basalt 2, Basalt 3. Used for questions 13 and 14.*

How many violent volcanic activities have taken place in the area?

*Options as printed:* A) Three   B) Two   C) Five   D) Six
questions.corrige_markdown:
A violent (explosive) eruption throws out fragmented material (ash, pumice, lapilli) that settles as pyroclastic deposits, whereas a quiet (effusive) eruption pours out fluid lava. In Figure 5 the **tuffs** (ash deposits) and the **ignimbrite** (deposit of a pyroclastic flow, or nuee ardente) are the products of explosive eruptions, and the erosional surface between them shows that they are two separate events. The three **basalts** are lava flows, the product of quiet effusive eruptions (the vesicles at their tops are the gas bubbles of fluid lava), so they are not counted. There are therefore **two** violent volcanic activities. (The thin unlabelled hatched band below Basalt 1 is not counted.)

**Intended answer: B (Two).**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 5 (the same figure as for question 13).

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: sequence of volcanic rocks, from the base: Tuffs, Ignimbrite (an erosional surface is marked at the top of the Tuffs), a thin unlabelled hatched band, Basalt 1, Basalt 2, Basalt 3. Used for questions 13 and 14.*

The vesicles in basalts 1, 2 and 3 were most likely formed as a result of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Magma contains dissolved gases (water vapour, carbon dioxide, sulphur gases). When the lava reaches the surface the pressure falls, the gases come out of solution as bubbles which rise to the top of the flow, and as the lava cools and solidifies the bubbles are **trapped**, leaving round or oval cavities, the vesicles, in the upper part of each flow. Fast cooling alone does not make vesicles (it gives glass or a fine grain), and the cavities are not formed by trapped liquid 'fluids' (C).

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Escape of volatiles from the lava

questions.enonce_markdown:
An igneous rock X was analyzed as having the following chemical composition. Study the information given below and answer questions 15, 16 and 17.

| Oxide | Per cent |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ | 50 |
| $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ | 3.2 |
| $\mathrm{CaO}$ | 11.7 |
| $\mathrm{FeO}$ | 6.0 |
| Others | 29.1 |

If this rock is phaneritic, identify the rock:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The percentages add up to $50 + 3.2 + 11.7 + 6.0 + 29.1 = 100\%$. A silica content of 50 per cent places the rock in the **basic** class (about 45 to 52 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$), rich in calcium and iron. A phaneritic rock is coarse-grained (the crystals are visible to the naked eye), so it is a plutonic (intrusive) rock: the coarse-grained basic rock is **gabbro** (its fine-grained equivalent is basalt). Granite is acid (more than 66 per cent silica), diorite is intermediate (52 to 66 per cent) and peridotite is ultrabasic (less than 45 per cent silica, with very little calcium).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the composition of the igneous rock X given for question 15.

What are the most likely essential minerals of this rock?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rock is a gabbro (question 15). Gabbro consists essentially of **calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar (labradorite)** and **pyroxene (augite)**, with olivine in the olivine gabbros. This is the association of option B. Andesine and hornblende (A) are typical of diorite, olivine and pyroxene (C) without feldspar form peridotite, and quartz, micas and feldspars (D) are the minerals of granite.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An igneous rock with an intergrowth of quartz and plagioclase feldspars displays a:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The intergrowth of quartz and plagioclase, in which quartz forms small wormlike (vermicular) bodies inside the plagioclase, is the **myrmekitic texture** (myrmekite, common in granites and granodiorites). The graphic texture is an intergrowth of quartz with alkali feldspar (orthoclase or microcline) in which the quartz looks like cuneiform writing; the poikilitic texture has small crystals enclosed in a large crystal of another mineral; the granophyric texture is a fine micrographic intergrowth of quartz and alkali feldspar.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Pelean type eruptions are characterized by:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Pelean type of eruption, named after Mont Pelee (Martinique, 1902), is produced by a very viscous, gas-rich lava which plugs the vent and forms a dome. The collapse or explosive failure of the dome sends down the slopes the **nuees ardentes** (glowing avalanches, incandescent pyroclastic flows of hot gas, ash and blocks). Liberation of volatiles (A) and release of dust and pyroclastic material (D) occur in all explosive eruptions and are not specific, and a Pelean eruption is strongly explosive (B is wrong).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Release of volcanic dust and pyroclastics

questions.enonce_markdown: Basic igneous rocks are rich in oxides such as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Basic rocks (gabbro, basalt) have a low silica content (about 45 to 52 per cent) and are made of ferromagnesian minerals (olivine, pyroxene) and calcium-rich plagioclase, so they are rich in **MgO, FeO and CaO**. Option A contains $\mathrm{K_2O}$, which is characteristic of acid rocks; option B has $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, which is abundant in acid rocks; option C lists sodium, characteristic of the more acid plagioclases.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A type of marble formed by the thermal metamorphism of limestone with some content of silica is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
When an impure limestone containing silica (quartz) is heated by an intrusion, calcite and quartz react to give calcium silicate: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3 + CO_2}$. The new mineral is **wollastonite**, so the rock is a **wollastonite marble**. Periclase, brucite and forsterite marbles come from dolomitic (magnesium-rich) limestone: periclase from the decomposition of dolomite, brucite from the hydration of periclase and forsterite from dolomite with silica.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the sketch below (Figure 6), which shows metamorphism at a plate boundary, and answer questions 21 and 22.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: sketch of metamorphism at a plate boundary (an oceanic plate descending beneath a volcanic mountain, sea on the left; dashed zones labelled P near the descending plate, O in the small zone with dark blobs under the volcano and Q in the large zone around it). Used for questions 21 and 22 (the printed text says 26 and 27 by mistake).*

The type of metamorphism that occurs at Q is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Figure 6 shows an oceanic plate being subducted beneath a volcanic arc. Three metamorphic zones are drawn: P, a small zone along the contact of the plates where the rocks are crushed under high pressure (dynamic metamorphism, high pressure and low temperature, blueschist facies); O, the small zone around the dark blobs of magma (contact metamorphism); and Q, the **large volume of rock** between the descending plate and the base of the volcano, which is buried deep and subjected to both high temperature and directed pressure over a wide area: this is **regional (dynamothermal) metamorphism**, typical of convergent plate boundaries. Shear metamorphism is a local, mechanical effect along fault zones.

**Answer: C.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

Used for questions 21 and 22 (the printed text says 26 and 27 by mistake).*

A rock formed by the type of metamorphism at O is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
O is the small zone round the dark blobs of magma under the volcano: the heat of the intruding magma bakes the surrounding rock without directed pressure, which is **contact (thermal) metamorphism**. Contact metamorphism of clay-rich rocks (shale, mudstone) produces the hard, fine-grained, non-foliated rock **hornfels**. Gneiss is a banded rock of regional metamorphism, and greenschist and blueschist are regional or high-pressure rocks (blueschist forms in the subduction zone, at P).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An outcrop pattern produced by folding and subsequent erosion in which younger beds form the core is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
After erosion of a fold, the beds in the core of a **syncline** are the youngest (the beds dip towards the axis, and the outcrop of the youngest bed lies at the centre, with older beds on each side). In an anticline or a dome the core is the oldest. An outlier is an area of younger rock completely surrounded by older rock (it can be left by erosion of a syncline or of a flat-lying cover), and an inlier is an area of older rock surrounded by younger rock.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 below illustrates three types of faults labelled X, Y and Z. Study the diagrams carefully and answer questions 24 and 25.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Figure 7: three block diagrams of faults labelled Fault X, Fault Y and Fault Z (Fault Z is a section showing a dark bed cut by a low-angle fault). Used for questions 24 and 25.*

The fault types X, Y and Z respectively are:

*Options as printed:* A) Normal, oblique, hinge   B) Reverse, strikeslip, thrust   C) Pivot, oblique, thrust   D) Normal, dipslip, pivot
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Fault X the dipping fault plane leans towards the block on the right, the hanging wall, and this block has been displaced upwards relative to the footwall: this is a **reverse fault**. In Fault Y the two blocks have slid past each other along the strike of the fault, a **strike-slip** (transcurrent) fault. Fault Z is a section where a low-angle fault plane has pushed older beds over younger ones, a **thrust**. Option B is the only one that fits this reading.

**Intended answer: B (Reverse, strikeslip, thrust).**

The type of stress responsible for the formation of fault X is:

*Options as printed:* A) Shear stress   B) Tensional stress   C) Compressional stress   D) Lithostatic stress
questions.corrige_markdown:
Fault X is a reverse fault (question 24): the hanging wall has been pushed up over the footwall, which shortens and thickens the crust. This happens when the rocks are squeezed horizontally by **compressional stress**. Tensional stress, which stretches the crust, produces normal faults; shear stress produces strike-slip faults; lithostatic stress is the uniform pressure of the overlying rocks, which does not by itself produce faults.

**Intended answer: C (Compressional stress).**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which two minerals in basalt will likely produce haematite upon chemical weathering?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Haematite, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$, forms when iron-bearing minerals are oxidised. The iron-bearing minerals of basalt are **olivine** $(\mathrm{Mg,Fe})_2\mathrm{SiO_4}$ and **augite** (a pyroxene containing $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$), which oxidise to haematite (and goethite) and give the red-brown colour of weathered basalt. Labradorite (a calcium-sodium plagioclase) contains no iron and weathers to clay; biotite is not an essential mineral of basalt; hornblende is rare in basalt.

**Answer: A.**

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: histogram of particle size analysis of a sediment (mass per cent from 0 to 100 on the vertical axis; particle size in mm on the horizontal axis: 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25). The 2 to 1 mm class is about 78 per cent; the other classes are each below about 10 per cent. Used for questions 27 and 28.*

In terms of sorting the sediment is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Almost all the sediment (about 78 per cent of the mass) lies in a single size class (2 to 1 mm), and each of the other classes is below about 10 per cent. A sediment in which the grains are nearly all of the same size is **well sorted**. A poorly sorted sediment would have its mass spread over many size classes with no dominant class.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 8 (the same figure as for question 27).

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: histogram of particle size analysis of a sediment (mass per cent from 0 to 100 on the vertical axis; particle size in mm on the horizontal axis: 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25). The 2 to 1 mm class is about 78 per cent; the other classes are each below about 10 per cent. Used for questions 27 and 28.*

From which environment is the sediment most likely to have been derived?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sediment is a well-sorted, medium to coarse sand (mostly 1 to 2 mm). Waves and swash on a **beach** winnow the fine particles away and leave a well-sorted sand. Alluvial fans receive poorly sorted gravel, sand and mud deposited by floods; glacial deposits (till) are the most poorly sorted of all, with boulders to clay; the deep marine environment receives fine silt and mud, with sand only in turbidites.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An isolated table-land area with steep sides is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **mesa** is a flat-topped, steep-sided isolated hill (table-land) left by erosion where a resistant horizontal bed protects the softer rocks below; when it is smaller and taller than wide it is called a butte. A rock pedestal is a mushroom-shaped rock in a desert, a zeugen is a ridge of hard rock capped by a resistant layer, and a yardang is a streamlined ridge cut by wind abrasion and aligned with the wind.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the thin-section sketch below and answer this question.

![fig-9](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

*Thin-section sketch of a sandstone (printed as a second 'Figure 3'; there is no Figure 9 in the paper): legend of quartz grains, feldspar grains and rock fragments set in a clay matrix, scale bar 5 mm. Used for question 30.*

What type of sandstone is represented in the figure above?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sketch shows mostly quartz grains together with some feldspar grains and rock fragments, all **embedded in a clay matrix** (the matrix, labelled in the legend, fills the spaces between the grains) and the grains are of very different sizes (poorly sorted). A sandstone made of quartz, feldspar and rock fragments in an abundant clay matrix is a **greywacke**. A quartz arenite is nearly pure, well-sorted quartz with little matrix; a litharenite is dominated by rock fragments; an arkose has more than 25 per cent feldspar and little matrix.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following sedimentary structures is indicative of a deep marine environment?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Graded bedding** (grains passing upwards from coarse at the base to fine at the top) is produced by turbidity currents, which carry sediment down the continental slope and deposit it in deep water (turbidites). Ripple marks (A) form in shallow water or rivers, an imbricate structure (C) is the shingled arrangement of pebbles in river gravels, and a Neptunean dyke (D) is a sediment-filled fissure in a rock, formed in shallow water, and is not diagnostic of deep water.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An organic limestone composed of the remains of Protozoa is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Protozoa are single-celled organisms, and the group with a hard calcareous test that builds limestone is the foraminifera: the rock made of their tests is a **foraminiferal limestone** (the nummulitic limestone is an example). A reef limestone and a coral limestone are made of corals and other reef builders (animals of the phylum Cnidaria and other groups), and a coquina is a limestone made of broken shells (mostly molluscs).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Lamellibranchs are distinguished from other molluscs by their:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Lamellibranchia (bivalves) have a body which is **laterally compressed** (flattened from side to side), protected by two valves, a left valve and a right valve, joined by a hinge and by a ligament. The gastropods have an asymmetric body coiled in a spiral shell, with torsion of the body (C and D describe gastropods), and the body of a bivalve is not compact and heart-shaped (A).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which feature of a Graptolite can help in determining its mode of life?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A graptolite colony (rhabdosome) began with a conical sicula, from whose apex a thin thread, the **nema**, extended. The nema gives the clue to the mode of life: when it is long and was attached to a float or to floating seaweed it shows a planktonic (floating) life, and when it ended in a disc or an attachment structure it shows a life attached to the sea floor or to an object. The thecae (A) housed the zooids, the rhabdosome (B) is the whole colony and the virgella (D) is the spine of the sicula; they do not by themselves tell how the colony lived.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below, which shows a Trilobite, and answer questions 35 and 36.

![fig-10](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

*Figure 10: a trilobite (dorsal view): head shield with a broad pitted fringe, small thorax and tail shield. Used for questions 35 and 36.*

Which of the following modes of life is best adapted to the Trilobite above?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The trilobite of Figure 10 is *Trinucleus* (question 36): a blind trilobite with a broad, pitted fringe round a flat head shield, a small thorax and a small tail shield. It lived on the soft muddy sea floor, crawling on the surface, and the pitted fringe is thought to have spread its weight on the soft mud. This is a **benthonic epifaunal** mode of life (living on the sea floor). Planktonic or nektonic trilobites have spines or large eyes for floating or swimming, and an infaunal burrower has a smooth streamlined body.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 10 (the same figure as for question 35).

![fig-10](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

*Figure 10: a trilobite (dorsal view): head shield with a broad pitted fringe, small thorax and tail shield. Used for questions 35 and 36.*

Identify the Trilobite drawn above.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The drawing shows a head shield (cephalon) with a very broad fringe pierced by rows of small pits and by long genal spines, a small thorax and a small pygidium, with no eyes: this is **Trinucleus**. Dalmanites has large eyes and a long tail spine, Paradoxides has a large head and a long thorax with many segments, and Deiphon is a small spiny trilobite with a globular head.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A rock contains a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 20 million years. Careful analysis shows a quarter of the original concentration of the parent isotope is left. How old is this rock?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A quarter is $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2$, so the parent isotope has gone through two half-lives:

$$
\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/t_{1/2}} = \frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = 2
$$

$$
t = 2 \times 20\ \text{million years} = 40\ \text{million years}
$$

An age of 20 million years (A) would leave one half, 80 million years (B) one sixteenth, and 5 million years (D) would leave about 84 per cent.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What phenomenon can be used to describe a particular marine lithologic unit outcropping and extending from the Douala Basin down to the Kribi/Campo Basin in Cameroon yet giving different ages?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A rock unit defined by its lithology which is followed over a distance and found to have **different ages in different places** is a **diachronous** unit, and this property is **diachronism** (time-transgression): for example, a sandstone deposited on a shoreline that moves seaward or landward through time is older in one place and younger in another. Uniformitarianism is the principle that the present is the key to the past, correlation is the matching of rock units or time of deposition between areas, and 'lateral discontinuity' is not the name of this phenomenon.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The periods of the Upper Palaeozoic in increasing order of age are:

*Options as printed:* A) Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian   B) Permian, Carboniferous, Devonian   C) Carboniferous, Devonian, Permian   D) Triassic, Permian, Devonian
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Upper Palaeozoic has three periods, which follow each other in time as: **Devonian** (about 419 to 359 million years ago, the oldest), **Carboniferous** (about 359 to 299 million years ago) and **Permian** (about 299 to 252 million years ago, the youngest). The Triassic belongs to the Mesozoic, which eliminates option D. The expression 'increasing order of age' is ambiguous: it is usually understood here as the chronological order from the oldest to the youngest period, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian (A); strictly read (older and older) it would be Permian, Carboniferous, Devonian (B).

**Intended answer: A (Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the sketch map below (Figure 11) and answer question 40.

![fig-11](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)

*Figure 11: sketch geological map with a legend: younger rocks (dotted and circled ornament) separated by the wavy line of an unconformity from an older series (limestone bricks, sandstone dots, shale dashes). Used for question 40.*

Identify the type of unconformity shown on the map above.
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the map the older series (limestone, sandstone and shale) outcrop as inclined bands, whose strike and dip are different from those of the younger rocks (conglomerate and sandstone) which rest on them: the boundary of the younger rocks cuts across the older beds and truncates them. When the older rocks are tilted or folded and eroded before the younger beds are laid on them, the contact is an **angular unconformity**. In a parallel unconformity (disconformity) the beds above and below are parallel, and a non-depositional unconformity (paraconformity) has no visible erosion; 'heterolithic unconformity' is not a standard term.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following determines the symmetry of a fold on a geological map?
questions.corrige_markdown:
On a geological map a fold is **symmetrical** when the beds on the two sides of the axial trace have the same dip and the same width of outcrop, and **asymmetrical** when the dips are unequal (and the widths of outcrop differ): the symmetry is therefore given by **the dip values and the width of the outcrop** on the two limbs. The rock types (A) only tell which beds are involved, the strike (B) gives the trend of the beds, and the thickness of the beds (D) fixes the width of the outcrop only together with the dip.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The dip values and width of outcrop

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following lithospheric plates is entirely oceanic?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Nazca plate**, off the west coast of South America, carries only oceanic crust (as does the Pacific plate, which is not offered). The African, North American and Eurasian plates all carry both continental and oceanic lithosphere: they include the continents Africa, North America and Eurasia.

**Answer: B.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is a diagrammatic section of different plate boundaries (Figure 12).

![fig-12](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

*Figure 12: diagrammatic section of different plate boundaries (oceanic plate, ridge, descending slab and volcanic arc, with letters V, W, X and Y). Used for question 43.*

Identify the main geologic feature formed at X.
questions.corrige_markdown:
At X the two oceanic plates move apart: this is a **divergent (constructive) plate boundary**, where hot mantle rises, melts and adds new basaltic oceanic crust, forming a submarine volcanic mountain chain with a central rift: the **mid-oceanic ridge**. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge (A) is one particular mid-oceanic ridge, which is not indicated by a general diagram, 'Ocean Ridge' (B) is not the standard name, and an island arc (D) forms by subduction (a convergent boundary), as at the right-hand side of the diagram.

**Answer: C.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: The Andes mountain was formed by the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Andes are a mountain chain along the western edge of South America, built where the dense oceanic **Nazca plate is subducted beneath the continental South American plate** (ocean-continent convergence). The compression folds and thrusts the edge of the continent, and the melting of the descending plate feeds the volcanoes of the chain. The Pacific plate does not collide with the Asian plate in this way (B), the collision of India with Asia (C) built the Himalayas, and the Nazca and Pacific plates are separated by a divergent boundary (D).

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: A relatively impermeable formation which can neither contain nor transmit water is called?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The terms are defined by how much water the rock can hold and transmit. Option B is printed 'Aquifage', a misspelling of **aquifuge**. An **aquifuge** is an impermeable rock which has no interconnected pore spaces, and therefore neither contains nor transmits water (massive granite or unfractured basalt). An aquiclude is saturated with water (clay, for example) but does not transmit usable quantities; an aquitard transmits water only very slowly; an aquifer holds and transmits water in useful quantities.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following constitutes the reservoir rocks of the Douala - Kribi Campo basin?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sandstones of the **Logbaba Formation** (Late Cretaceous, typically Campanian to Maastrichtian in age) are the classical reservoir rocks of the Douala basin (the Logbaba gas field of Douala takes its name from them). The Nkappa and Souellaba formations are generally described as shale- and marl-dominated units, which act as source or seal, and the Isongo Formation belongs to the Rio del Rey basin (the Niger Delta type succession).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 13) shows a vertical section through a weathered sulphide ore body. Study the diagram and answer questions 47 and 48.

![fig-13](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)

*Figure 13: vertical section through a weathered sulphide ore body with Zone 1 (top cap), Zone 2 (arrows pointing down), Zone 3 (stippled band) above the water table, then Zone 4 and Zone 5 below it; Zone 5 is marked Primary Sulphides. Used for questions 47 and 48 (the printed text says 42 and 43 by mistake).*

In which zone is supergene enrichment most likely to take place?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a weathered sulphide ore body, oxygenated water percolating down through the upper zones leaches the metals (Zones 1 to 3, above the water table). Below the water table, where the environment is reducing, the dissolved metals are re-precipitated as secondary sulphides (for example chalcocite and covellite), which raises the metal content: this is **supergene (secondary) enrichment, in Zone 4**, just under the water table. Zone 5 holds the unaltered primary sulphides (labelled in the figure), and Zones 2 and 3 are the zones of leaching and oxidised minerals above the water table.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 13 (the same figure as for question 47).

![fig-13](gce-al-geology-2026-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)

*Figure 13: vertical section through a weathered sulphide ore body with Zone 1 (top cap), Zone 2 (arrows pointing down), Zone 3 (stippled band) above the water table, then Zone 4 and Zone 5 below it; Zone 5 is marked Primary Sulphides. Used for questions 47 and 48 (the printed text says 42 and 43 by mistake).*

Which of the following processes is characteristic of zone 3?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Zone 2 is the zone of leaching and solution (the arrows show the solutions moving down). Zone 3 is the stippled band just above the water table, where the metals carried down by the solutions come out of solution and **are deposited** (precipitated), as oxides, carbonates and sulphates (for example malachite and azurite for copper). Oxidation (B) is the process which starts at the surface, in Zones 1 and 2, leaching (C) and solution (D) characterise Zone 2.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a primary volcanic hazard?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Primary volcanic hazards are the direct products of the eruption: lava flows, ash fall, volcanic gases, bombs and **pyroclastic flows (nuees ardentes)**. A lahar (volcanic mudflow, A) forms when ash is remobilised by rain or by melting ice, a landslide (B) is caused by the instability of the slopes and a flood (C) comes from water or melting ice: these are secondary hazards.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following rocks is commonly used as an armour stone?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Armour stone is the large blocks of hard, dense, strong and durable rock which are placed on breakwaters, sea walls and river banks to resist the wave energy. **Granite** is the standard example: it is hard, has a low porosity and resists weathering and abrasion. Slate (A) splits easily along its cleavage, gneiss (D) breaks along its foliation, and basalt (B) is mostly used as road aggregate and building stone (it is also used as armour stone where granite is not available).

**Answer: C.**
themes: engineering geology and quarry site selection
